Pick a move under Here, read the odds, then tap **Try it**. Line up help on the phone while you travel, but a call can fail and an answer takes hours.

People who help you give you cards, and a card works on its own. It lowers the number you need on the die, or lets you try a move at all, at the stops its help reaches. The party's cards stop working at the border, and some people only move for money.

Each turn, answer your phone, make up to one call, then make one move. Police attention rises while Sosā searches where you are, and at 10 the police stop you; each stop within 12 hours of the last is worse, and the third step is house arrest. Get out of Esmeraldan airspace inside 72 hours.
To install on an iPhone: tap Share, then Add to Home Screen.

The route and the people on it
Saturday, 2 p.m. You lost the election, and the court has barred you from leaving Valdória. Your second passport is in your coat.

Two unmarked cars sit outside the house in Portô Venla. Inspector Valentīn Sosā runs the departure inquiry from the Interior Ministry, and he is good at it. Rādiô Portô Venla has you on a yacht in the harbor, which is where you want him looking.

Your brother or sister is abroad finding a jet, and no crew will book until they can say where it is going. A sponsor in another country will ask a ministry for your visa, for a price. Rosario Vélez, aide to Esmeralda's interior minister, can have people waiting at the border if Baca gets your name in time. Gianlūka Moretī runs the party. He can put a mayor, a judge or a border post on the phone, and he writes down every call.

Nando has driven you for 11 years. Nonā Rosa Trentinī has a room in Nova Trentô, a phone, and a grandson who knows which boxcar the guards skip. Holt Greer works the midnight freight out of Salta and sells his chalk-marked crate to anyone with cash. Theo Bascom runs the yard. Two of the people helping you already work for Sosā, and which two changes every run.

South through Santa Laura, where the posts have not received the travel ban yet. East to the colônia at Nova Trentô. Up to the rail town at Salta and onto the midnight freight over the Huhūi passes. Three crossings lead into Esmeralda there, a day apart. One of them has taken Valdória's money, and you find out which when the sergeant walks into the hut with your passport and does not come back. Past the line is Susana, a charter apron behind the port, and a pilot who flies where the flight plan says.

Where it says is the first thing you decide. Lāyūna in Atlanta, where Amādū Salek wants the family accounts moved to his bank before he picks up a phone. Almatau in Tarun, where a magistrate named Dēvan Rāo answers by letter and takes six hours longer. Gannibal in Zaryanova, where Mirēlā Vosk wants mineral rights you do not control. Whichever you pick will take you.

A call takes hours, a move takes a roll of one die, and police attention climbs toward 10 while Sosā searches where you are. At 10 the police stop you. The first stop is questions, the second is a night at the station, and the third is house arrest, unless 12 quiet hours pass between stops. You have 72 hours, Saturday afternoon to Tuesday at 2 p.m.

Or sit at Sofīā Leōnī's desk. She is aide to the incoming minister, who wants a location by Tuesday, and she works with the watch team, the Santa Laura desk, a yardmaster who takes money from anyone and tells her about it, and an embassy in Baca that will ask Esmeralda to hold the candidate. Her orders stop at the border, and her reports come in hours old, some of them wrong.

The demo is one scripted escape with a coach beside you, 20 steps, and there is a shorter one for the government side. In the daily run everyone starts from the same draw, so you and a friend can compare endings. It is one page that works offline once loaded and saves your run. It is hard on purpose, and one bad call on Saturday evening can end it before it starts, so when a 20-minute run ends you start another.
Valdória, Esmeralda, Atlanta, Tarun and Zaryanova are countries of the Nelosphere, Ron Bronson's fictional world, written since 1991, and they stand on real ground.
